meanings.note: Common everyday verb for offering or asking for assistance.

examples.trans: I am going to help you.

meanings.note: Used for signing contracts, forms, and leases.

examples.text: Ele não quer assinar o contrato.
examples.trans: He does not want to sign the contract.

meanings.note: Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Used with de + infinitive ('capable of doing').

examples.text: Meu tio não é capaz de assinar um contrato.
examples.trans: My uncle is not capable of signing a contract.

examples.text: Ela é capaz de resolver tudo.
examples.trans: She is capable of sorting everything out.

meanings.note: Diminutive of certo, very common in tudo certinho ('everything all set').

examples.trans: It already leaves everything all set.

examples.text: Está tudo certinho com o contrato.
examples.trans: Everything is all set with the contract.

meanings.note: Legal agreement or rental lease.

examples.text: Meu tio não quer assinar um contrato.
examples.trans: My uncle does not want to sign a contract.

meanings.note: Versatile core verb; dando falsa esperança means giving false hope.

examples.text: Ele está dando falsa esperança pra nós.
examples.trans: He is giving us false hope.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Loanword used across Brazil for graphic, product, or fashion designers.
Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: A business or employer.

examples.text: E a empresa onde você trabalha?
examples.trans: And the company where you work?

meanings.note: Expectation or wish for something good.
Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Agrees in gender and number with the noun.
Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: A printed or digital document with fields to fill in.

examples.text: Vou preencher o formulário pro senhor.
examples.trans: I will fill out the form for you, sir.
Sign the form at the bottom.

meanings.note: Self-employed contractor working without a fixed company contract.

examples.text: Não tenho empresa, eu sou freelancer.
examples.trans: I do not have a company, I am a freelancer.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Doubled as já, já, it means 'very soon / any minute now'.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.
I have already been in that situation.

meanings.note: In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: I’ll go to the meeting soon.

meanings.note: Informal Rio and Brazilian slang for 'cool, awesome'.
Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Between article and noun (a mesma coisa) it means the same.

examples.trans: We work on the same team.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: One written contraction of em + essa. Feminine singular because reunião is feminine; at is natural English for attendance at a meeting.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
First-person plural pronoun used after prepositions like pra.
Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Literally 'obliged'; men say obrigado and women say obrigada.

examples.trans: Thank you very much, you hear?

meanings.note: Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
False friend: means any family relative, not specifically 'parent' (which is pais).

examples.text: Não tem outro parente, um tio?
examples.trans: Don't you have another relative, an uncle?

poder.gloss: can; may; to be able to

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Standard verb for completing a form or document.

examples.text: Faço questão de preencher o formulário.
examples.trans: I insist on filling out the form.

meanings.note: A person's trade or career.
Asks someone to identify one item or role, as in qual é o seu cargo.
All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: In fazer questão de, means to insist on doing something.

examples.text: Eu mesmo faço questão de preencher.
examples.trans: I myself insist on filling it out.

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Polite title; saying sim, senhor to an equal coworker adds mock military obedience.

examples.trans: Are you going in now, sir?

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: A state of affairs or circumstance.

examples.trans: I have already been in that situation.

meanings.note: Everyday friendly farewell across Brazil, borrowed long ago from Italian ciao.
Informal singular object pronoun, routinely mixed with você in warm everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Brother of one's parent.

examples.text: Não tem outro parente, um tio?
examples.trans: Don't you have another relative, an uncle?

meanings.note: Neutral pronoun for 'everything / all of it'.

examples.text: Vai ficar tudo bem com ele.
examples.trans: Everything is going to be fine with him.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Gerund vendo pairs with estar (tá vendo, do you see), and tem que ver means we have to look into it.

examples.text: Você tá vendo aquela moça ali?
examples.trans: Do you see that young woman over there?
